title: fibonacci goes large
prompt:
Compute the fiftieth Fibonacci number. It is 12,586,269,025, which is the point: that does not fit in 32 bits, so this loop is why the `x` registers exist.

Keep the classic sliding pair: `a` and `b` start as 0 and 1, and fifty times over, the new value is `a + b`, then the pair slides forward. When the loop ends, `a` holds the answer.

## what is checked

- `fib(50)` printed on its own line
- the program exits cleanly
- the loop builds it (answer not written in)
starter:
// the fiftieth fibonacci number will not fit in 32 bits
define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)

define(a_r, x19)
define(b_r, x20)
define(next_r, x21)
define(i_r, x22)

        .data
fmt:    .string "fib(50) = %lld\n"

        .text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        mov     a_r, 0                      // fib(0)
        mov     b_r, 1                      // fib(1)
        mov     i_r, 0

        // TODO: fifty times over, advance the pair: the new value is
        // a + b, then a takes b's place and b takes the new value.
        // When the loop ends, a_r holds fib(50). This is why the
        // aliases live in 64-bit x registers: the answer needs 34
        // bits.

        ldr     x0, =fmt
        mov     x1, a_r
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret
